posts.hook: Tuesday, 9:40 p.m., a new client searches your shop name on their phone.
posts.body:
Tuesday, 9:40 p.m., a new client searches your shop name on their phone.

The only thing that comes up is your Facebook page, and the last post is from March. No prices. No hours. No way to book.

They close the tab and book the shop two doors down.

You don't need a fancy site to fix this. You need one page that answers three questions: what you do, what it costs, and how to book. Put your address and phone number on it too, and make sure they match your Google listing.

If you're not sure what that page should say, start there.

posts.hook: Search your business name on your phone right now.
posts.body:
Search your business name on your phone right now.

Look at what comes up first, then check four things:

1. Is there a web address, or only a Facebook page?
2. Can a stranger see your services and what they cost?
3. Can they book or ask for a quote without messaging you?
4. Does the phone number match the one on your truck?

If you answered no to any of these, that's your first fix. A simple site can cover all four.

posts.hook: The truck is parked at the courthouse, and someone asks for the menu.
posts.body:
The truck is parked at the courthouse, and someone asks for the menu.

Plenty of food truck owners believe a social feed is enough. It isn't, quite. A feed buries your menu, your hours, and next week's location under old posts, and a stranger has to scroll to find them.

A single page with those three things answers the question before anyone asks it.

posts.hook: Your phone rings at 4:15 while you're under a car.
posts.body:
Your phone rings at 4:15 while you're under a car.

You can't pick up, and the caller doesn't leave a voicemail. They call the next detailer on the list.

Here's the honest question: what happens to that lead after you miss the call? If the answer is nothing, the job goes to whoever replied first.

Most people calling about a detail want a time and a rough price. A reply that goes out within minutes, even an automatic one that asks for the car and their preferred day, keeps the conversation alive while you finish the job.

How long does it take you to reply to a message you missed?

posts.hook: Before: a homeowner texts on Friday at 6 p.m. asking about a recurring clean.
posts.body:
Before: a homeowner texts on Friday at 6 p.m. asking about a recurring clean.

You see it Saturday, mean to answer, and by Monday they've booked someone who replied first. Their details end up in a notebook you don't open on weekends.

After: the same text gets an instant reply that asks for the home size, the start date, and the best phone number. Those details land in one list. Saturday morning you get a note of what's waiting, and you reply that morning instead of on Monday.

Same customer. Same job. The difference is who takes the first step.

posts.hook: Tonight, take ten minutes and write down the last three messages you never answered.
posts.body:
Tonight, take ten minutes and write down the last three messages you never answered.

Include missed calls and the Facebook or Instagram messages that sat there.

Next to each one, write what the person wanted: a time, a price, or a yes or no. Those three lines show you exactly what's slipping through.

Then pick the one that would cost you the most if it stayed quiet, and decide what the first reply should say. One fix is enough to start.

posts.hook: Saturday, 9:00 a.m., the chair by the window is empty.
posts.body:
Saturday, 9:00 a.m., the chair by the window is empty.

Nobody called to cancel. The client just didn't come, and the slot is gone.

You spend the next hour texting people from memory, hoping someone can move up.

Then you remember the reminder you meant to send Friday night. You didn't have time, so it never went out.

A reminder that goes out on its own the day before takes that memory off your plate. Your clients still get the text. You just stop being the one who has to send it.

posts.hook: The 9 a.m. meeting starts without the client, again.
posts.body:
The 9 a.m. meeting starts without the client, again.

Many owners think appointment reminders are a nice extra for a bigger office. A missed hour hurts a two-person practice just as much as a twenty-person one, and a missed hour is often what a reminder would have prevented.

A confirmation sent the day before, with the time and an easy way to reschedule, lets the client answer on their own schedule. Start with the appointments you miss most, then build from there.

posts.hook: Tonight, open tomorrow's calendar and count the showings.
posts.body:
Tonight, open tomorrow's calendar and count the showings.

Next to each one, write whether the client has confirmed in writing.

Any showing without a confirmation is the one most likely to leave an empty house and a locked door.

Send those confirmations yourself tonight, in ten minutes, or decide which messages you want going out automatically from now on. Either way, the list is the starting point.

posts.hook: Before: a catering order comes in on Messenger at 9 p.m.
posts.body:
Before: a catering order comes in on Messenger at 9 p.m.

The date, the headcount, the address, and the phone number go into your notes app. Friday morning you copy them into a receipt book, then type them again to confirm. One digit gets flipped, and nobody notices until the truck is already parked.

After: the order is captured once, from the message itself. The date and address go to the same place as your schedule. You get a reminder before you leave, and the customer gets a confirmation without you retyping anything.

Same order, same customer. The copying is what changes.

posts.hook: Write down every place you type the same customer's name this week.
posts.body:
Write down every place you type the same customer's name this week.

Check each one:

1. The booking app or calendar
2. A Messenger or Instagram reply
3. Your invoice or receipt tool
4. A notebook, spreadsheet, or sticky note

If a detail shows up in more than two places, it's a candidate to automate. Start with the one you retype most. A form that feeds a spreadsheet is a simple first step, and the help pages for Google Forms explain how to set one up.

posts.hook: Who types your customer's address into your system, and when?
posts.body:
Who types your customer's address into your system, and when?

If the answer is you, at the end of a long day, the usual mistake is a transposed digit or a missing unit number.

Then the crew drives to the wrong place, or the invoice goes to an old email. The fix is often simple: have the customer enter it once, in the form they already use, and let it flow from there.

Would you want to know how many times it was retyped this month?

posts.hook: Last Monday the bank statement had a charge for a booking app nobody has opened since spring.
posts.body:
Last Monday the bank statement had a charge for a booking app nobody has opened since spring.
Your front desk thought the manager was paying it. The manager thought the old stylist set it up. Nobody was sure who could cancel it.
That is how a small shop ends up paying for tools nobody uses. The charges keep coming a little at a time until someone reads the card statement line by line.
Pull the last few statements this week. Circle every recurring charge. Next to each one, write who uses it and what it does. If nobody can answer, that is your first cancellation.

posts.hook: The renewal email came on a Tuesday, the same week the free trial ran out.
posts.body:
The renewal email came on a Tuesday, the same week the free trial ran out.
Before you let it renew, check three things yourself.
Who signed up, and which email address did they use?
Has anyone opened the tool in the last month?
Does a tool you already pay for do the same job?
If you cannot answer all three, find out before it renews. Cancel from the company's own cancellation page, then save the confirmation email. Check your card next month for any charge that keeps coming.

posts.hook: Who on your team would notice if one software charge stopped tomorrow?
posts.body:
Who on your team would notice if one software charge stopped tomorrow?
If the answer is nobody, that charge deserves a closer look. A subscription can start with one person's free trial and never get an owner.
The card keeps paying long after the person who signed up has moved on. The cost is quiet. It is not one big bill, just a line nobody claimed.
Find one recurring charge you cannot explain this week, and ask who started it.

posts.hook: Everyone in the shop knows the booking password, so it must be fine.
posts.body:
Everyone in the shop knows the booking password, so it must be fine.
That is the belief. Here is what is true. A shared password cannot be changed without breaking every device that uses it, and you cannot tell who used it on a bad day.
Trusted people still leave. Phones get lost. Passwords end up on sticky notes by the register.
Give each person their own login. Turn on two-step sign-in for the booking system and the shop email. When someone leaves, you turn off one account instead of changing everything.

posts.hook: Before: the old cleaner's login still worked the Friday after she quit.
posts.body:
Before: the old cleaner's login still worked the Friday after she quit.
Nobody noticed until a customer asked about a message that had been sent from her account.
After: each cleaner has a personal login. When someone leaves, the owner turns off that one account the same day. Two-step sign-in is on for the shop email, so a stolen password alone is not enough to get in.
The rest of the crew keeps working with the same tools, and nobody else has to change anything.

posts.hook: Tonight, look at who can still get into your shared email.
posts.body:
Tonight, look at who can still get into your shared email.
Open the admin page for your email account and read the list of users. Remove anyone who no longer works with you, including old assistants and past partners.
Then turn on two-step sign-in for every account that can reset another account. Do the same check for the folder where your listings and contracts live.
If you find an account you do not recognize, change its password before you do anything else.

posts.hook: The invoice looked exactly like the last one from the lumber supplier.
posts.body:
The invoice looked exactly like the last one from the lumber supplier.
Same logo, same amount, same signature. The only change was a new bank account at the bottom.
The office manager paid it that afternoon. Later that week the supplier called, asking where the money was.
This kind of scam works because the email looks normal. Before you pay any changed bank details, call the supplier on a number you already had, not the one in the email. Ask them to confirm the new account.

posts.hook: Before you pay anything with new bank details, check three things yourself.
posts.body:
Before you pay anything with new bank details, check three things yourself.
1. Call the vendor on a number you already had, not the one in the email.
2. Ask who requested the change, and confirm it with that person by phone.
3. Compare the amount and invoice number with the last bill you paid.
If any of these does not match, stop. Do not reply to the suspicious email to ask about it. A real vendor will not mind the call. A scammer will push you to hurry, and that pressure is the warning sign.

posts.hook: Would your bookkeeper notice if a supplier's bank account changed this week?
posts.body:
Would your bookkeeper notice if a supplier's bank account changed this week?
These scams often copy a real supplier's email, so the only thing that looks different is where the money goes. By the time someone notices, the payment has already left.
Ask who has the authority to change where bills get paid, and whether that change needs a phone call first. Write the answer down before the next invoice arrives.

posts.hook: The laptop slid off the passenger seat on the way to a job and hit the curb.
posts.body:
The laptop slid off the passenger seat on the way to a job and hit the curb.
The screen cracked and the drive would not start. Every customer address, every photo of finished work and every scanned contract was on it.
Nothing had been copied anywhere else. That evening the owner rebuilt the client list from texts and memory.
A backup is a second copy stored somewhere else, and it only counts after you have restored something from it. Check when your last backup finished, then ask yourself when you last opened a file from it.

posts.hook: Before: the only copy of every listing photo lived on one desktop in the back office.
posts.body:
Before: the only copy of every listing photo lived on one desktop in the back office.
When the hard drive failed, the photos were gone, and reshooting them was the only option left.
After: the important files copy automatically to a second location away from the office. Someone tests a restore on a schedule, so the copy is known to work. There is a written order for what to bring back first.
The computer can still fail. Now it is an inconvenience, not a loss.

posts.hook: Tonight, pick one file from your backup and try to open it.
posts.body:
Tonight, pick one file from your backup and try to open it.
Choose something you would hate to lose, like a signed contract or a year of invoices. If it opens, write down where that copy lives and who can reach it.
If it does not open, you just found the problem before you needed the file. Then answer one more question: if this computer disappeared right now, what would you restore first?
If you cannot answer that, write it down this week.

posts.hook: Sunday night, a customer emails asking for a quote, and the price sheet is on the shop computer.
posts.body:
Sunday night, a customer emails asking for a quote, and the price sheet is on the shop computer.

The shop computer is locked in a building you left at six. So the reply waits until Monday, and by Monday the customer has booked someone who answered faster.

This is the one-desk problem. The business only moves when you sit in front of one machine. The fix is not a faster computer. It is making your files and email reachable from a phone or laptop, with logins only you and trusted people can use.

Start small. Write down the three documents you reach for most, and make sure they can be opened from anywhere.

posts.hook: Before you drive away from the job site tonight, check your phone.
posts.body:
Before you drive away from the job site tonight, check your phone.

Ask yourself these four questions:

Can you open the current estimate template without going back to the office?

Can your crew see tomorrow's schedule without calling you?

If you were sick tomorrow, could someone else reach the invoices?

Does your login ask for a second step, like a code sent to your phone?

If any answer is no, that's your first project. You don't need a new system to fix it. Pick the one thing that would cost you the most money if it stopped, and make it reachable tonight. Keep a second copy somewhere other than your truck.

posts.hook: Who else could open your business files tomorrow if you were out sick?
posts.body:
Who else could open your business files tomorrow if you were out sick?

Be honest about it. Most owners think about this only after something breaks. The listing folder, the signed agreements and the client list often sit on one laptop, behind a password only one person knows.

That setup works until the day it doesn't. A flat tire, a hospital visit or a dead phone, and the whole deal stops with you.

A business should keep running on a normal day off. A reachable, backed-up set of files is what makes that possible. Nobody should have to be a hero to keep a closing on schedule.

posts.hook: Myth: you need a full binder before your process is worth writing down.
posts.body:
Myth: you need a full binder before your process is worth writing down.

What's true is smaller. Start with the one job that goes wrong when you're not in the chair. Maybe it's the color mix, the booking rules for new clients, or how you close the shop on Saturdays.

Write those steps in plain words, the way you would explain them to a new hire standing next to you. Five short steps beat a binder nobody opens.

Then test it. Hand the steps to someone on your team and watch where they get stuck. Fix the gap, and keep the page where people can find it.

posts.hook: Monday, the new hire calls you four times before the first job starts.
posts.body:
Monday, the new hire calls you four times before the first job starts.

Where is the bleach? Which rooms get the green cloths? Do we vacuum before or after the kitchen?

That was the old way. You trained by walking them through each job, and every answer lived in your head.

Now the same training looks different. There is one page per job type with the steps in order, a checklist for the walk-through, and a note on what to do when a client asks for something unusual.

The new hire reads the page, asks a question or two, and starts. You stop re-explaining the same job every time someone joins the team.

posts.hook: Tonight, take ten minutes and write down the one job only you can do.
posts.body:
Tonight, take ten minutes and write down the one job only you can do.

Don't pick the biggest job. Pick the one that stops everything when you're away.

Use a plain list. Name the task, the tool it uses, the login it needs, and who would do it if you couldn't. Describe the way you actually do it, not the way the manual says it should be done.

Tomorrow, put that list somewhere your team can open it. A shared folder or a printed page on the wall both count.

Once that first page exists, the next job is easier to hand off, and the one after that is easier still.

posts.hook: Can you name every app and subscription your business pays for this month?
posts.body:
Can you name every app and subscription your business pays for this month?

Try it right now, from memory.

Most owners get through the big ones and stall on the rest. The website host, the card reader, and the scheduling app from a free trial that quietly became a paid plan. Some of those charges are for tools nobody has opened in a year.

That isn't a failure. It happens when a business grows one tool at a time, and each decision made sense on its own.

The useful question is simple: which of these do we actually use every week? The answer shows what to keep, what to cancel, and what is missing.

posts.hook: Things to gather before you ask anyone for a quote on new computers or software.
posts.body:
Things to gather before you ask anyone for a quote on new computers or software.

List the devices your crew uses, including phones and the old laptop in the back office.

List the accounts: email, bank, card processor, website, and who owns each login.

Note what happens today when something breaks. Who do you call, and how long can the business run without it?

Note every monthly charge, even the small ones.

Then ask for quotes. You'll get answers you can compare against your own list instead of guesses. If you can't fill in the list, that's a sign the first step is a review, not a purchase.

posts.hook: Myth: the business needs new software before anything else.
posts.body:
Myth: the business needs new software before anything else.

What's true is that a new tool added to a setup nobody has mapped usually makes the mess harder to see. Before you buy, know what you already own and which logins exist.

Then check the basics. Are the files backed up automatically? Does every login ask for a second step? Who do you call when the internet goes out?

Those answers decide what to fix first. Sometimes the first fix is cancelling something you pay for and don't use.

posts.hook: Before: the same reply to the same question, typed again tonight.
posts.body:
Before: the same reply to the same question, typed again tonight.

Are you open Saturday? What's the cut time for a fade? Do you take walk-ins? Each answer is correct, and each one costs you a few minutes.

After: a saved draft answers the questions people ask most. You read it, change the one detail that is different today, and send it. It still sounds like you, and you stop retyping the same paragraph every evening.

Two rules keep it safe. Check every price and time before it goes out, because a draft can be out of date the moment your schedule changes. And don't paste customer details into a tool until you know what it does with what you type.

posts.hook: Try this on your next proposal: let an AI tool write the first draft.
posts.body:
Try this on your next proposal: let an AI tool write the first draft.

Give it your notes, the scope you agreed to, and the tone you want.

Then do the part it can't do for you. Check every number, date and price against your own records. Read any legal wording line by line, or have someone qualified read it before it goes out.

Remove anything you didn't actually promise. A confident-sounding draft can include details that are wrong.

Finally, take out client names, account numbers and personal details before you paste anything in. The outline and the scope are usually all the tool needs.

posts.hook: Myth: a tool that says it is private is private.
posts.body:
Myth: a tool that says it is private is private.

What's true is that you have to read what it does with what you type. Does it keep your messages? Does it use them to train its models? Does it share them with other companies?

Look for those answers in the terms, not on the homepage. If a company plans to start using your data in a new way, it should tell you clearly and ask first.

Until you know, keep client phone numbers, card details and appointment history out of the box. Use it for drafting the sign on the wall or a thank-you text, not the client file.
